title: India Joins US and 13 Economies in Joint Push Against Global Industrial Overcapacity
excerpt: Fifteen economies signed a USTR-released statement targeting state-backed overproduction in autos, batteries, semiconductors and solar — with China notably absent and India itself under a separate US trade probe.
body:
• India joined the United States and 13 other economies in signing a Joint Ministerial Statement on October 7 calling for coordinated action to eliminate structural excess capacity and end "non-market policies and practices" that distort global trade.
  • The 15 signatories — including the EU, Japan, South Korea, Canada, Australia, Mexico and the UK — will set up dedicated sectoral platforms covering automobiles and EVs, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors and solar panels.
  • China, Brazil, Indonesia, Russia, Saudi Arabia and South Africa did not sign; the G20 trade ministerial in Milwaukee had failed to reach consensus on the issue.
  • India signed even as it faces its own US scrutiny: New Delhi is among 16 economies covered by a separate USTR Section 301 investigation into excess capacity launched in March.

India has joined the United States and 13 other economies in a joint push against what they call structural excess industrial capacity, signing a ministerial statement that takes aim at state-backed overproduction — a diplomatic broadside widely understood to be directed at China.

The Joint Ministerial Statement, released by the Office of the US Trade Representative on Wednesday, was signed by 15 economies: Argentina, Australia, Canada, the European Union, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Mexico, Poland, Türkiye, the United Kingdom and the United States. It followed discussions among G20 trade ministers in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on September 30 and October 1, and was finalised on the sidelines of OECD Trade Committee deliberations in Washington.

What the statement says

"And watch Beijing's response: China has historically treated such groupings as containment by another name."

The signatories call on all countries "to take steps to eliminate structural excess capacity and production in their economies, including by ending the use of non-market policies and practices that distort markets and contribute to the problem." They warn that, absent such steps, "an increasing number of countries are taking action to defend their industries, workers, and economies" — a nod to the tariffs and trade barriers already proliferating — and argue that coordinated, complementary action would be more effective than going it alone.

The group will establish dedicated sectoral platforms to exchange information and explore action in five sectors of concern: automobiles and electric vehicles, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors and solar panels — precisely the industries where Chinese overcapacity has flooded world markets and triggered defensive measures from Washington to Brussels to New Delhi.

Who stayed out

The absences are as telling as the signatures. China, Brazil, Indonesia, Russia, Saudi Arabia and South Africa — all G20 members — did not sign. The G20 trade ministerial itself failed to reach consensus on excess capacity and forced labour, which is why the 15 moved ahead with a separate statement. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that over the course of the US G20 presidency, numerous economies had raised instances of capacity "sustained by foreign governments' non-market policies and practices" — language that avoids naming China but describes its industrial model.

India's delicate position

India's signature carries an irony: New Delhi is itself under American scrutiny on this exact question. India is among 16 economies covered by a separate USTR investigation launched in March under Section 301 of the US Trade Act, examining whether excess manufacturing capacity connected to government policies harms US commerce. India has maintained that its manufacturing capacity is geared to meet both domestic and global demand, and experts say New Delhi must balance cooperation with its own Make in India ambitions — particularly in semiconductors, batteries and solar, where India is actively subsidising domestic capacity.

Still, India has more to gain than lose from the grouping. As a country trying to position itself as the alternative manufacturing base to China — a shift already drawing Japanese and American firms — joining the statement aligns New Delhi with the world's biggest importers and gives it a seat at the table when the sectoral platforms set the rules.

What to watch

Statements are cheap; the test is the sectoral platforms. Watch whether the 15 move from information-sharing to coordinated remedies — joint anti-dumping action, shared subsidy registers, or common standards for EVs and batteries. And watch Beijing's response: China has historically treated such groupings as containment by another name. The Section 301 investigation, meanwhile, remains the sharper instrument — its findings could land on India's own doorstep.
